speakerposition: Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: The hon. gentleman (Mr. Carvell) ought to know ; he was out stumping.

I do not vote in either of these provinces, but I take the hon. gentleman's word as to the election. As I have said, members of the opposition are getting scared. About a week ago, the Minister of Customs (Mr. Paterson) tried for three or four days to get Supply to pay the salaries of the officers of his department. In the course of that discussion, the hon. member for Leeds said :	Withdraw sections 1 and 17 of the Election Bill and we will give you Supply in a few minutes. But then they found that there was an immense vote in Ottawa dependent upon that Supply for a living. And they got scared-and virtuous. And now their cry is : For God's sake, give these people their money ; we have voted it why don't you give it to them ? Then, it was stated that no militia camps could be held because there was no money. And these hon. gentlemen got scared again, and I should imagine from the statement made by the Minister of Militia (Sir Frederick Borden) that they are begging him : For God's sake, hold the militia camps. They are very anxious that all votes of Supply that can benefit them should be put through, but they will refuse to grant any thing that will not secure votes for their side. The action of these hon. gentlemen raises the question fair and square: Can the government of this country, whether Liberal or Conservative, afford to be placed in such a position as that ? Can any government afford to place itself at the mercy of an opposition and virtually declare that, if the opposition do not like any thing contained in legislation that is introduced, all the opposition has to do is to withhold Supply and the government will back down ? carried out in practice and you have a country ruled not by the majority but by the minority. The facts in this

case are very short. About Starch 1, a Bill was Introduced providing for amendments to the election law. In the first week in Stay the second reading of this Bill was moved and the opposition opposed it. I am not going to discuss the merits or demerits of that Bill. Nor will I deny the right of the opposition to oppose a Bill that they believe to be unjust. But I do say that they have not the constitutional or moral or equitable right to say : Unless you will withdraw those provisions of the Bill which we regard as objectionable, we will deprive the Ottawa civil servants, the contractors, every man or woman who is paid by this government throughout the Dominion of their pay. There is no use trying to get away from it; there is no use in these hon. gentlemen saying : We will let you pay the Customs officials for fear we shall not get their votes in the pending election : take the money to hold the militia camps for fear we may not get the votes of those interested. These hon. gentlemen would like to get away from this, but we will hold them to it-the plain question is whether this country is to be ruled by the majority or by the minority. Concede what these hon. gentlemen now contend and you establish a precedent under which any future opposition can demand the withdrawal of any section of any Bill under threat of withholding Supply. Can any government, I say, afford to be placed in that position ? Will the people of Canada justify any government in allowing itself to be put in that position ?
It is no wonder the members of the opposition are trying to recede from this position. The course they took during the last week shows that they are trying to recede' from it. They persistently obstructed Supply for three or four days over the vote to pay the civil servants in the Customs Department, then they gave in. Ever since then they have, by foolish and silly questions, delayed the granting of Supplies for hours, and finally have allowed one or two small items to go through in order that they might be able to say to the country : We are not blocking Supplies. Take their course last night. The Minister of the Interior brought in a resolution to grant $200,000 for the payment of certain salaries. I am willing to admit that the hon. member for Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk) had a right to ask the question with which he started the discussion, I am willing to admit that probably a quarter of an hour could be reasonably spent in the discussion of that question. After that, we had a spectacle which would not be tolerated in any other parliament of any civilized country in the world-we had three hours of obstruction, three hours taken up in every possible way, from the leader of the opposition down to the hon. member from Mae-
donald (Mr. Staples), for three hours and a half all sorts of silly questions were asked, and finally they granted the $200,000.

I want to ask the hon. gentleman who says : ' Down to the hon. member for Macdonald,' does he not think that the questions which the hon. member for Macdonald asked last evening are quite as intelligent as the stuff he is getting off at the present moment 1

If the hon. member wants an honest answer I shall have to tell him that I do not think so, and I think that every honest member of parliament on either side of fhe House will agree with me in my conclusion-except possibly the hon. member himself. Now, Sir, when ,the next item came up, as I said before, what did the opposition do ? They deliberately blocked Supply, and then allowed the item to pass so that they might go to the country and say : We did not block Supply, because we gave you the $200,000. I ask again: Can any self-respecting government afford to be placed in this position ? I say there is only one solution to this question ; if this opposition, or any other opposition, chose to pursue such a course, the inevitable consequence will be the closure. I am not the firs;t one to advocate the closure. I am going to quote to the hon. gentleman an authority coming from their own party, I am going to quote to them an article from the Montreal ' Gazette ' of Juue 1, in the form of an editorial, a portion of which reads as follows :
It is not the use, but the abuse of the right of discussion that creates public weariness and leads people to upset the natural order of things and to think of the government which acts as of more importance .than the parliament that only talks. So, probably, the mass of the people, without knowing much about the situation, would approve of a plan which promised to shorten the session of parliament by checking the flow of unreported talk, Closure began in the French parliament. It was adopted by that of Great Britain. It exists in the Congress of the United States. These are in their way the three leading parliamentary bodies in the world. What they have agreed to accept may be expected to come in other popularly ruled countries.
To my mind that is the proper doctrine.
I am sorry that it has become necessary that we should discuss the question of closure. Hon. gentlemen opposite, and more especially the hon. member for Leeds (Mr. Taylor), have tried to show that this is not the first time Supply has been blocked in this parliament in order to prevent obnoxious legislation going through, and they have referred to the conduct of the Liberal opposition in 189(1. But I want to tell .the hon. member, and he knows I am telling him the truth, that it is not a parallel case at all. The records of this House can prove that there was no blocking of Sup-

ply. As a matter of fact parliament expired by effluxion of time on the 24th of April, and Supply was granted up to the 1st day of July following. The opposition gave the then government Supplies up to the first of July, and there was plenty of time between the 24th day of April and the 1st day of July within which to hold an election, to call parliament together and vote Supply. Therefore, I say that is not a parallel case. It is just as well that the people of this country should know that it is not a parallel case, and I hope the members on this side of the House will not forget to show the people that it is not. I am glad this question is beginning to be agitated. I am much obliged to the hon. member for Northumberland (Mr. Owen) for bringing on this discussion. It is a question that needs to be discussed, it is a question on which the people should have more light. I think the people ought to know that if the civil servants cannot get their pay, if contractors, cannot get their pay, if the railway navvies, as the hon. member for Leeds calls them, cannot get their pay, if the merchants andj others from whom the government purchase supplies cannot get their pay, the people ought to know who is responsible for it. The idea of talking such nonsense as some hon. gentlemen do here, that they are not blocking Supply ! I ask you, Sir, has there been an instance since this session began on the 28th of November last, when the government have asked for Supplies that they have not been met by an organized system of obstruction ? I am safe in saying that in nine-tenths of the cases where the House has been moved into Committee of Supply they have been met by some sort of a ridiculous resolution, in many cases pressed on to a vote ; if not pressed on to a vote, then by a ridiculous discussion, such as we have witnessed the last fortnight. The whole day has been taken up by discussion, and then along about midnight we get into Supply. Still hon. gentlemen opposite get up and say they have not blocked Supply. Take the last month. While the Minister of Public Works was trying to get his estimates through, we sat here might after night' while they were blocking Supply, and towards the small hours of the morning perhaps one or two small items would go through. Now they come down and say : We are not blocking Supply, we want the employees of the Customs Department to get their pay, we want the militia to get their pay. But while they say so, all the time they are blocking Supply. Then they find fault with the Minister of Finance because he does not come down w'ith a Supply Bill every oilier day, while they are only willing to allow a small item of $200,000 to get through in the course of a day. It is just as well that the people should know
who it is that is blocking Supply. Let me give you two instances of what occurred when I was in New Brunswick last week.
I met two contractors, one of them doing some work for the Grand Trunk Pacific, and another building a wharf in the county of Northumberland. Both of them have progress estimates amounting to thousands of dollars ; and although they have been obliged to borrow money from the banks, although they have incurred liabilities while doing the work for the government, they could not get a dollar. Why ? Because this loyal opposition won't allow them to have it, and because this opposition hare deliberately pursued this policy of obstruction and have refused to let the estimates go through. They want to stop the construction of every public work in Canada, and it is just as well that the people should know upon whom to lay the blame. The blame is to be laid at the doors of the opposition, and not at the doors of the government. Therefore I say that this is a matter which ought to be discussed thoroughly ; and I believe that if the opposition determine to persist in this unpatriotic, unworthy course, the next move the government will have to take is to adopt the closure. And I now say to the government that in my opinion, while I think that is the only course they -can pursue, it is one that will be sanctioned and approved by the people of this country. Let the government start in at once to change the rules of this House, if it takes months to do it, in order to adopt the closure. While I say this, I do not claim that the opposition have no rights ; I admit they have rights in this House, they have rights in every parliament. They have a right to discuss any question, they have a right to ask questions when the government are asking Supply and they are entitled to all possible information, but there is not a man of them, except the hon. member for Lincoln (Mr. Lancaster), who has intimated that the government have withheld any information which would justify them in taking the course they have taken. They have a right to discuss all these questions and then they have a further right to demand a vote upon any item ; but that is all they have a right to do, and the people of Canada are justified in asking that they shall he reasonable and when they have exhausted these rights allow the business of the country to proceed. Therefore I repeat .that it is useless for them to attempt to withdraw from the position. Either they have to takei the position that they will block Supply deliberately, as the hon. member for Lieeds (Mr. Taylor) has done and stand by it and be responsible or take the other course and say : We will act constitutionally, we will discuss these questions as they should be discussed and when we have discussed them to that extent we will vote against

these measures and leave it to the people to say whether we have acted rightly or wrongly.
I feel that this is a matter of such importance that we should hear from more members on this side of the House. I feel further that it is up to the government, to use a slang expression, to take more drastic measures than they have in the past unless this policy of deliberate obstruction is withdrawn in a very short time.

We have listened to quite a lecture from the hon. gentleman who has just sat down. We are not unaccustomed to it, as during this session there has been hardly a day that some hon. junior member of the Liberal party has not seen fit to tell the opposition how they should Conduct the affairs committed to their hands. For my part I prefer to be guided by the advice of those in whom I have confidence and by my own judgment. I have been absent from the House for a couple of days and have met a great number of intelligent people, Liberal and Conservative, and I venture to say that the voice of the people has come back to the members of the government and they know pretty well what they are up against now, and so, as the hon. member for Carleton, N.B. (Mr. Carvell) has just said, they are glad of an opportunity of speaking to-day and so they may be. The government to-day realize that if they can possibly get any excuse for talking anil beclouding the issue until after the elections in Ontario and Quebec, it is better to do so than even to get Supplies through. Who are obstructing to-day? Who but the Minister of Finance and those w-ho, at his instance, have taken up the time of the House. Was any hon. gentleman on this side opposed to going into Supply? Is there anything to prevent us, except the organized system which has developed among the supporters of the government, from going into Supply? I understand that in my absence Supply has been granted from day to day, and there is no reason, so far as I know, why we should not have been in Supply at 11.30 this morning, had it not been for the excited and unnerved speech of the Minister of Finance, followed by the long and in some cases utterly irrelevant speeches of hon. gentlemen who support him. Now that the Minister of Finance should be unnerved and excited is not surprising. If he knows the pulse of the people of Canada to-day it would be surprising if he was not unnerved and excited. If he could calmly, as a statesman, reason the questions that come up from time to time in his old time way it would be surprising to me. He' knows perfectly well that the current of public opinion has set so strongly against the government that it is absolutely necessary they should resort to any plausible excuse for tiding over

the difficulties pressing on them, pending the two elections which they know will have such an important bearing on the election they will soon have to face themselves. They want to try and modify the feeling of want of confidence that exists in the electorate to-day. The fact is that the government are at sixes and sevens on almost every point they have to deal with, and that they are so on this very question of Supply is perfectly evident from the statement of the Minister of Finance to-day. Tile Minister of Finance would like the House to understand that the Minister of Customs was right in his statement that he was prevented by the action of the opposition from paying the 1,800 officials in his department. On May 26 at 3 o'clock in the morning an item of $1,705,000 was brought up for us to vote. To show you that the Minister of Finance has not one leg to stand on in his contention that there is anything to prevent those 1,800 people from being paid, I refer to the ' Hansard ' and find that an hour and a half later, at the close of the discussion, the minister said :
I want to pay these men to-day. This is the day that we issue our cheques. We do not want them to be delayed, we want to issue our cheques if possible to-day and we want you to grant this item of $1,705,000.
And so it was recognized that iif we would grant Supply the money would go immediately to these employees. On the 29th, the next time it came up, the greater part of the item having gone through, he said :
Let the whole item go through because I do not think I can use a part of it. I do not know that the Auditor 'General will issue the cheques unless the whole item is passed.
Therefore he pleads to let the amount go through. The leader of the opposition said that it would be no harm to let it stand until Monday when the minister would have the cheques. The minister said:
Yes, but it is discriminating between the inside and the outside service. But will I get it on Monday so I can issue the cheques?
He was told that he could in all probability and he received the amount which was granted on the statement that it was necessary to issue the cheques at once and that the Auditor General would allow the cheques to issue as soon as the item was approved of by this House. And so he would have done if he had confidence in the administration. But it appears by the press that the Auditor General does not see his way under present conditions to allow it unless the Supply Bill passes. The leader of the opposition said at that time :
Let the $40,000 item stand.
Mr. FIELDING said :

No, it would stop the whole item. The several items constitute one resolution, so that there would he nothing to report.
But now, when they find that the Auditor General, for reasons that are sufficient to himself and in which he may be perfectly justified, refuses to allow the cheques to issue until the Supply Bill is introduced and passed, these gentlemen assume another attitude. Why do they not bring down a Supply Bill ? They have brought down Bills for infinitely smaller matters than this, and there is no reason why they should not bring in a Supply Bill. As a matter of fact, I claim it is absolutely their bounden duty to introduce a Supply Bill at once. They have made the statement that we were preventing the holding of militia camps. They know that we were never asked for a vote for that purpose and when we ask them to take action they hesitate. They do not know what they want or do not want, but meantime slander the opposition by innuendoes and statements in their press.
Is it worth while to introduce a Supply Bill? Let us see what we have passed within a little more than half a month. On May 15 we passed $533,000 of estimates for the Minister of Public Works. On May 20 we passed estimates amounting to $1,101,975. On May 22 we passed $5,479,110, a pretty big day's work. On May 29 and June 1 this item of the Minister of Customs was completed and by it we have passed $1,815,187 which, with the amount already passed, made a total vote on that item of $2,074,075. On June 2 we passed $198,548 and on June 3 we passed $216,293. Not counting the hundreds of thousands of dollars we passed yesterday we have in 15 or 16 days at six sittings of the House voted $9,347,113, and that money is immediately available for the government and' for the men.

speakerposition: Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Just one-quarter of the annual expenditure under the Conservative government.

That may not appear a great deal of money to these gentlemen opposite with their -wild ideas of expenditure and ghastly extravagance, but under ordinary circumstances it is a very large sum. And they can add to that within 24 hours, because if they bring down any reasonably non-contentious items they will be passed at once. There is no disposition on the part of the opposition to absolutely block Supply, but in view of the disclosures we have had this session, last session, and the session before, the government has shown itself absolutely undeserving of the confidence of the people and in the public interest the opposition must carefully scrutinize these expenditures. The Minister of Finance has again reiterated the statement that the opposition have no rights except such as the majority at his back see fit to concede and the member for Yale-Cariboo has endorsed that statement, while the member for Carleton (Mr. Carvell) has adopted a more rational view. Well Sir, it will be a poor day for Canada and it will be a wretched opposition when the opposition will consult the government of the day as to what they shall do and how they shall criticise the expenditures of the country and the policy of the government. It is the duty of the opposition to guard [DOT] the public treasury, to watch closely the progress of public business, to scrutinize the acts of the government, and in the honest discharge of that duty there should be no hard and fast rule laid down to bind them. The opposition are to-day only too anxious to take the verdict of the people of the country on whether they have been faithfully discharging their duty, and on whether the government should fbe allowed longer to remain in power. I have very great respect for the hon. member for East Kent (Mr. Gordon) both in his personal and public capacity, but I must say that he had a very ungracious task assigned to him this morning by some members of the government in having to go through an argument in which he evidently took no interest and which I doubt very much that he himself appreciated. I venture to say that no one in the House thinks that argument of the hon. gentleman had any relevancy whatever to the practical issues we are discussing today. The hon. gentleman said that the opposition had on occasions come out in their war paint, and he asked why should they use 100 ton guns to shoot flies. Well, I would like to know that too. Look at the flies on the other side of the House. It used to be flies on the wheel but now it is flies on the run or 'it will be as soon as the people of Canada get a chance at them. When the time comes that these gentlemen on the other side of the House are sitting in opposition, and that time will be soon if we can judge of the public sentiment, I wonder if they will advocate the principles we hear them advocate to-day. You talk about killing time by delivering long and irrelevant speeches, as being obstruction, and yet the supporters of the government are the chief sinners of this session. For some purpose or other they have been constantly delivering important speeches which have had no relevancy to the question before the chair, and this I attribute to the fact that the government were not ready with public business, and so their supporters had to come to their aid and cause delay. Where is the Civil Service Bill, so long promised ? Where is the Land Bill ? It was introduced just one week ago although we had it up last session and presumably the government should have introduced it the very first day of this session ; but it has been delayed until the

7th month. It is an intricate Bill and one which will require to be well considered and discussed. It is no secret that on these questions with regard to which we on this side are opposed to government, there have been dissensions amongst the supporters of the government themselves, -want of harmony in their ranks-and therefore in order to get time to bring the warring factions of the Liberal party together the government has delayed its jneasures. * Does the Minister of Finance think that we are going to enter a blind pool every time he asks us. He wanted one-quarter of the total Supply without the items being discussed and the leader of the opposition granted him one-eighth. After lettihg the whole time run until, as the Minister of Customs said, the last day for payment of these officials had arrived, they come and asked us to give another one-eighth, another blind pool. If we had granted that, they would have wanted one-Jialf, and we would have come practically *to the end of the session without one important item of legislation being brought down and the whole of the Supplies voted without our knowing what those Supplies covered. I protest against that. The hon. member for Carleton, New Brunswick, (Mr. Carvell) thinks we should be limited to a quarter of an hour in discussing important questions. I do not think we are to be told Jhat we are to have a quarter of an hour or half an hour or anything of that kind. We are sent here to be our own judges of the course we pursue. I put myself in the judgment of the people, and not in the judgment of the hon. gentlemen opposite as to what course is proper. Bach member .must judge for himself what course he should take on the various measures as they arise.

Does the hon. member adhere to the principle laid down by the hon. member for Leeds (Mr. Taylor) that the opposition will and ought to resist the granting of Supplies until the Election Bill is withdrawn?

That is just another illustration of the fact that the supporters of the government cannot appreciate either what the opposition say or what the trend of public opinion is in many cases. The hon. gentleman utterly fails to understand the significance of the argument of the hon. member for Leeds. The hon. member for Leeds, as I understand him, propounds this principle, that when an iniquitous measure is brought in, one that is far reaching in its consequence, one that is totally indefensible, one that should not be passed in the interests of the people as a whole, not some little side issue that affects a small number of people, but a great measure that affects the dearest rights and privileges of all Mr. LENNOX.
the people of Canada, the opposition should use every legitimate means in their power to prevent such legislation being passed.
Just one more question. Does the hon. member contend that the absolute refusal to grant Supplies is. a legitimate means of opposing the proposed legislation?

There are times when it would be quite proper for an opposition absolutely to refuse to grant Supplies, and I think we are probably approaching very close to that time now. I do not say that we are actually up against it. I say that when the government have acted in such a way all along the line that the opposition can have no confidence in their administration, and have no reason to believe that the public moneys will be honestly expended in the interest of the people, then we have reached a time when it is not only the privilege, but the incumbent duty of the opposition, to stand firm as one man and present a united front against the passage of any Supplies. I hope we won't come to that condition; but I do say, feeling the responsibility of my words as a member of this House, that we have approached perilously near it. I say, looking all along the line- of this administration, and seeing how it is marked by extravagance, and it does not stop at extravagance-by reckless extravagance-that would not describe it either-but by acts which I shall not characterize in tills House, but which are well known to the public-I say the administration of this government, in almost every department, is marked by things which indicate that the people have lost confidence in it; and the members of the House knowing more of their administration than the people outside, but not more than I hope the people will know very soon, I say it may become the duty of the opposition to stand firm as one man and refuse to grant Supplies to the administration. We are not at that point yet; we are not yet at the parting of the ways ; and, on the other hand, I think we ought to be almost at the point of granting Supplies this afternoon. I hope we will get into Supply now, unless as a matter of fact the government want to distract public attention unless they do not want anything done this afternoon. But if they want to tide over the first of next week, as I think they do, then we may expect that the suggestion of the hon. member for Carleton will be followed, and that we shall have more oratory from the government side of the House. Answering the hon. member for Carleton, New Brunswick, let me refer to other authorities on this question of withholding the Supplies. Sir Richard Cartwright, in 1896,"discussing a similar question, said :
