speechtext:
These gentlemen were responsible for the good government of the country while they occupied seats on the treasury benches. They knew perfectly well long before the 1st of April that there was not the ghost of a chance of tlieir getting the Remedial Bill through under any condition of things.
I pause there to say that these hon. gentlemen who Introduced the Bill that has been referred to, left it until the 9th of March and then until the 6th of May, and they knew perfectly well that there was not the ghost of a right to get it through under any conceivable condition of things.
They knew perfectly well that there was not a ghost of a chance of their getting their estimates through.
These gentlemen held this Bill back, and so created the same kind of difficulty as that which Sir Richard Cartwright is here dealing with, knew perfectly well that the fiscal year expired on the 31st of March, and they did not introduce this contentious Bill until the 9th of March.
They knew perfectly well when the fiscal year expired on the 1st of July that they could not get Supplies, as they had lost control of the parliament. .
Is there any doubt about this administration having lost the control of parliament? They have not only lost control of parliament, but the confidence of the people, and it is because they realize that to-day and do not know where they are at that they do not know what is the wisest thing to do. Whenever the Finance Minister gets up now to speak, he has lost his old time vigour and firmness and is utterly unnerved and unstrung, and talks in that exciting, uncontrolled, unmeasured style I so much regret to see.

speakerposition: Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Lost his head.

I will not say that; but he is going to lose his position very soon if we can get the general elections on. Sir Richard Cartwright went on to say :
What would honourable men have done in such a case? What would men imbued with the spirit of British usage and precedence have done? Why, Sir, they would have dissolved the parliament they could not control, and found out whether or not they did enjoy the confidence of the people of Canada.
Hon. gentlemen opposite suggested that they would dissolve parliament. They let it go out in the press that they would do so; but when the time came they had not the nerve to dissolve parliament, because they did not want a speedy trial and a speedy conviction. Further, Sir Richard said ;
More than that, they would have taken care to have dissolved in such time that they might
have had their elections early in May, and met early in June at the very latest, in order that parliament might deal with the questions which it was clearly impossible for parliament to have dealt with at the time I have referred to.
I have also under my hand utterances by the Prime Minister, but they are very voluminous. I will just take a statement of the Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Brodeur), whom I see in the House. He said :
'My remarks, Mr. Chairman, are quite relevant. il wish to point out that the government are unable to pass this Remedial Bill into law, that they no longer represent the people, that they no longer enjoy the confidence of the members of this House, and therefore, that parliament would not be warranted in trusting to them the expenditure of $1,000,000 to boodle with.
Hear, hear.

Sometimes we are called to order in this House. This hon. gentleman used the expression 'boodle' and applied it to the transactions of the government and was not called to order. He declared that the government of that day, which had been elected by a large majority, had so demonstrated their unfitness that he would not trust them with the expenditure of $1,000,000. Are we therefore to be censured for not being disposed to trust this government, whose disregard of all honesty and decency is so evident with the vast sums they are asking us to vote in the dark? I am prepared to vote Supply. We want to cooperate with the government in voting Supply. We have to call on them to bring forward the necessary -estimates-estimates in the interests of the people. Speaking for myself, I am not very much in sympathy with the remarks of the hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Carvell) regarding the contractors. The contractors are a dangerous element in elections. If this election Bill of the government is to go through, we ought to scrutinize these matters very closely. The distribution of large funds to contractors on the eve of the elections in Ontario and Quebec is very dangerous, and I am convinced it is better not to disburse these large amounts to contractors until after the elections. Of course I can well realize the anger and disappointment of some supporters and members of the administration over their failure to have the supplies voted before a general election. But if you will look along the line of the discussion, you will find that there has been no instance in which the opposition have been obstructing the passing of reasonable estimates. We have certainly demanded a certain amount of information, but the trouble is that when the opposition are

ready to grant Supply the government are not prepared to go on. Just as happened yesterday and the day before, whenever an offer is made to facilitate business, the government show that they are utterly unready. They realize that they are far behind with the necessary legislation-legislation they have promised and must pass this session if they are going to discharge their duties at all-and then they set up speaker after speaker to obstruct business and in this way tide matters over until after the provincial elections in Quebec and Ontario.

I do not very often trouble the House, and I can assure the gentleman who has just spoken that I have not been put up to obstruct legislation or delay proceedings. I was going to say a few days ago what I intend saying now, but unfortunately for myself I mentioned the election Bill and was ruled out of order. To-day however it is pretty hard to tell when one is out of order after what I have heard. I do not intend to mention the election Bill any more than to say a little about the position in which we are to-day. When I was a young man I joined a society, and one of the first things impressed upon my mind- and it was continually impressed upon me at the opening ceremonies-was that I should yield a cheerful compliance to the constituted majority. I had the idea, from my experience in societies and organizations of one kind and another ever since, that the majority should rule, and that when a man finds he is in a hopeless minority, he should fall in with the majority or at least give way when he sees he cannot get the majority to think as he does. But it is entirely the opposite in this House. There does not seem to be the majority rule here. When a certain Bill was brought into this House-I have to be very careful, but I assure you, Mr. Speaker, I am not going to discuss the Bill-which affected one or two provinces, all the representatives from the province to which I belong, were quite agreeable to the provisions of the Bill. They were agreeable at least to its going into committee, and in committee they would no doubt lend a hand in altering some of its provisions. But the majority from the province of British Columbia, which is one of the two affected, were quite agreeable that this Bill should pass its second reading. In the other province affected, seven of its representatives were willing that the Bill should be proceeded with but three objected. The opposition took up the view of those three and have proceeded on the assumption that those three gentlemen are possessed of brains of such a superior calibre that their opinion and judgment should have far more weight than the opinion and judgment of the other seven. Well, I do not think Mr. LENNOX.
that is at all in accord with our ideas of responsible government. Those men should have yielded cheerfully to the opinion of the majority-a majority elected in the same way as they were. In my province there was no protest against the election of any members. They were all elected in a straightforward manner so far as I know, and I have heard very little objection from my province to that particular Bill. Therefore I do not see why the House should be tied up as it is simply because three members from one of the provinces do not like the provisions of the Bill. But even if every member on the opposition side objected to the Bill, they are only one-half as many as those who are willing that the Bill should be proceeded with. We have heard a good deal about the opinion of the man on the street. Well, let the members of the opposition take the opinion of the general run of men on the street, and they will find that these men are wondering how a government, with so strong a majority, can be held up as this government has been for some time past. On this question of holding up, we find contradiction among our opponents. One section says that the government are not held up, that they are willing the government should go ahead, and that it is the fault of the government when they do not get ahead with their Supply. But one or two others threaten that the government will not get a dollar unless they drop that election Bill. AVhat are we to understand from this? My hon. friend from Leeds (Mr. Taylor) has told us that he had gone up and consulted his constituents and they instructed him to come down to Ottawa and fight this election Bill to a finish and that they would get up a subscription to pay his board bill, if he were not able to pay it himself, so that he might stay here until the snow would fly.

speakerposition: Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: That is the opinion of the man on the street.

I would like to ask :	Who are these people from Leeds?
It seems to me that my hon. friend from Leeds (Mr. Taylor) thinks the sun rises and sets in his constituency. I would like to ask him some day to follow the sun and proceed west, and he will find that it takes five days and nights on a railway train to find out where the sun sets in this Dominion. And he will find constituencies all along that line each one with just as intelligent a population as that of the constituency of Leeds, and who have sent a majority here who are as well able to form a judgment as any of the people of Leeds. We have been taunted this afternoon with taking up the time of the House and keeping the House from getting into Committee of Supply. I am not going to be guilty of that. I am one of the ' burjrnN"E 5, 1908
docks ' on the back benches-that, I think, is the elegant expression which was used by an hon. gentleman not very far from where I sit-I am not very often heard from nor do I obstruct or take up the time of the House. But I would ask the opposition to consider this matter seriously, to think for themselves how the man on the street is likely to view their proceedings in this House. It is wonderful the prophetic view of these gentlemen and how they can tell exactly how the people regard every matter and what is to be the result of the next election. But we have heard the same thing over and over again for many elections back. And still the results have come far short of what these hon. gentlemen would wish. I think that after the next election they will find the result about the same.

Like the last speaker, (Mr. Kennedy) I seldom address the House. Nor should I detain hon. members long. But there are times when even the quietest member in this House should rise in his place to protest against the way business is conducted. The question now under discussion was brought to the attention of the House this morning by the hon. member for East Northumberland (Mr. Owen) in a speech of five or ten minutes. And we have found hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House ready to carry that discussion along; every time a member on this side has risen to speak to-day, he has been answered in a long speech by an hoD. member from the other side. I was glad to hear the hon. member for East Kent (Mr. Gordon), for like myself he seldom troubles the House, and I am sure that his only reason for rising to speak was that he thought that what he was to say was of importance to the House and the country. Such a member should always be listened to.
Now, in the first place, when we came here-and it is nearly seven months ago- we expected that the work of this parliament would be ready to go on with. But what do we find after seven months ? We find that the most important legislation of the session is only now being prepared for our consideration. Could there be a more important subject, for instance, than the Hudson Bay Railway ? That is a subject that should be discussed here with the very greatest care. We should consider the course that road is to take, for it would be a very serious matter if it were built in the wrong position. My own opinion is after considering carefully all that has been said in the long discussion of the matter that the road should go directly from Prince Albert to Fort Churchill. Then, we have the Civil Service Bill-another question that will require time. In the third place, we have this disputed question in regard to the election law. All these things are being brought before us after seven months of
sitting? Why were these not all ready when we came here in November ? In the county of Huron we have a county council composed of business men and farmers, and I would undertake to bring them here and they would finish the business of this parliament, do everything that has to be done here, and do it well, in six weeks. I am ashamed to think that we have sat here all this time and accomplished so little. It is not that we do not go through the form of working, for we sit here such long hours that we actually endanger the health of members of the House. There is only one factory in this Dominion that I know of where the employees are expected to go to work at eleven o'clock in the morning and work until three or four the next morning, and that is this factory on Parliament Hill where we empty windbags and manufacture laws. I think that if we were to try to get our speeches into condensed and concise form, it would be much better. Why, Sir, Mr. Chamberlain has delivered some of the best speeches ever delivered in the British parliament in half an hour. And here we are on both sides-there is no use in finding fault with one side more than with the other-making speeches of four and five hours duration. Do you think any body will ever read them ? Do not you think that the people who read ' Hansard ' in after years will say that we spend forty times as long in expressing our ideas as we have any need to do? At the origin of parliament, you know, Mr. Speaker, the struggles that were gone through to establish the (rights and privileges of the body of representatives of the people. The sword, and even the stake and the axe, had to be met and overcome that we might have certain privileges and advantages. And I am sure that even the opposition has its rights that were gained in those struggles. I do not think that hon. gentlemen opposite should say that the opposition has no rights except such as the majority choose to allow them. In fact, I do not think they meant what they said. I was pleased to hear the hon. member for Carleton, New Brunswick (Mr. Carvell) admit that members of the opposition had some rights. This parliament takes up more time in legislating for six millions of people than is occupied by the British parliament in legislating for four hundred millions. I am only speaking for myself, but I should be very much pleased to see the speeches cut down. In the United States Congress, I understand, a member speaking on an amendment is limited to five or ten minutes. I think that it would be a good thing if our speeches could be made equally short. I believe also that the Speaker should leave the chair at twelve o'clock at night, just as he does at six o'clock in the evening. If these changes were made, I believe we should make better progress. It is some-

thing terrible what the members here are! expected to submit to. I came down here| from the county of Huron three years ago on the tenth of last January, and five of my neighbours came with me as members of this House. We were all strong, healthy men-I was the oldest and most worn-out man of the whole six. And where are the men now ? Three of them are dead and buried and other men sit in their places. We six were the representatives of the three Hurons, the two Bruces and North Wellington. All must have been strong able-bodied men, or we could not have gone through the labour's of a political campaign. But long hours, irregular meals aud worry did their work. Why, it would appear to be more dangerous to come to this parliament than it was to go to South Africa and fight the Boers-the death-rate here is much greater than it was there. Let me draw your attention, Mr. Speaker, to the fact that, since 1904, we have had the following deaths amongst us : Messrs. McCreary, McIntosh, Proulx, Clarke, Sutherland, Demers, Johnston, Prefontaine, Bland, Laurier, Martin, Stockton, Cochrane, Gunn and Lovell-fifteen men taken away in that short time. I have no doubt at all -and I am sure the medical men on the other side will back me up in this-that this room is an unhealthy place. We get here no direct sunlight ; and we know that sunlight is necessary for health. Take a potato and plant it in a cellar where there is no light, and though you may have moisture, good soil, proper temperature and all other necessary conditions, what will be the colour of the "stems ? The stems will be pale and sickly.
I think it would be well to change the rules of the House. For instance, we should have short, concise speeches. Let it be understood that when we have something to say we say it and then sit down. A gentleman about to address the House was asked how long he intended to speak on a certain subject, and he said, ' If I know nothing about it, it will take me three hours; if I understand it fairly well, I can get through in an hour; and if I know it perfectly well, I can get through in half an hour.' I think there are some members here who speak sometimes when they do not understand very well what they are talking about. I think there should be a time limit for speeches, with perhaps some way of giving a special privilege to members under certain circumstances. I think the rules of the House might be changed in that direction. I think also that the government should have their business ready when parliament opens so that we can get right down to work. The government cannot get out of this whole difficulty by trying to throw the blame on the opposition. A certain amount of blame may be attached to the opposition. I think, however, it Mr. T. CHISHOLM.
is a good thing we have a ' Hansard,' because that ' Hansard ' will show, this year's ' Hansard ' at any rate will show, that the members on the government side of thd House have taken up as much time as we have, aud perhaps more. There is no use denying what is put down in the ' Hansard.' All the important measures of the government should be ready at the beginning of the session. There is another thing we should not forget, the health of the members ought to be considered. If we are to be kept here so many months every year it will soon become impossible for a poor man to come here at all. In fact any man who has business, or anything to do outside this House, can scarcely afford to come here now, because he has to stay here so long that it spoils his business. We will not be able to get good men to come to parliament as long as the sessions are as lengthy as they are now. I formerly thought that all the men who come to parliament were great men, but I am obliged to confess that my opinion has undergone a considerable change since I came to this parliament. My idea was that we had here two hundred and fourteen men, the greatest men probably in the world, and I came to my first session in awe and trembling. I am beginning now to think that after all they are not such great men. But I suppose that is a consequence of my view point. Now I want to say also that long sessions are causing more deaths than used to take place when the sessions were shorter. I find that during the first ten years when the sessions were shorter, there were only twenty-five deaths, while during the last three years there have been fifteen deaths. It is, however, not only a question of health, but one of business. I hope therefore we will not go on in this fashion like a lot of school boys. I think if the government gave the back benchers a chance to settle this question, and allowed the front benchers to go off on a picnic, both the members of the government and the leaders of the opposition, we on the back benches could get together, and I am satisfied we woiild settle this whole thing and finish up in about two weeks. I did not get up to talk long, and I do not intend to transgress the rules that I am recommending the House to adopt.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Motion agreed to, and House went into Committee of Supply.
Contingencies in Canadian, British and foreign agencies, and general immigration expenses, including salaries of extra clerks at head office, $710,000.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I would like to ask the minister why this large appropriation, nearly three-fourths of the total $920,000, is offered to us under the item of contingencies? Is it not possible to give a more definite idea of the purposes to which this is

to be applied? I suppose It Is an old custom.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I do not wish to be held responsible for the method In which the item is placed before the House; as my hon. friend has said, it is an old custom. While it is possible that in many particulars the House might fairly be asked for a definite amount, on the other hand, it is a fact that the ex-pendiures covered by this part of the vote are variable in their character, owing to circumstances and conditions uncontrollable by the government. If the amount were divided up and apportioned to different purposes, it might be found that by reason of changed circumstances one item would be more than was necessary while another would fall short of the requirements. That is probably the reason that prompted the former government to present the estimates m that way. Of course, we are able to give a statement of the sum that has been voted for the former year, and to give to the House our expectations in regard to the sum that we ask the House to vote now.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I thoroughly agree that this particular item is one which embraces an extremely varied expenditure, but I would have thought that if you left $150,000 for contingencies it might meet the requirements. I would not press that very much if the minister with his experience in the department thinks it necessary to have the vote in this form. If he would, however, give the heads of expenditure last year and briefly the heads of expenditure this year, I think it would assist matters.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
If I might finish what I was about to say, generally we are able to state to the House our expectations or intentions in regard to the amounts we ask for, but in this item, if circumstances arise which render it unnecessary to make an expenditure, then when we get the bulk vote we are able to vary the expenditure, whereas if it were voted item by item we would not be able to make that variation, and it would necessarily result in a very much larger total amount being required to be voted so that all possibilities of change would be guarded against. The amount asked for this year is the same as was asked for last year. Of that amount the estimates that we make as to the expenditure as follows :	Advertising, printing
pamphlets, &c., $178,000. This is for advertising in Canada, the United States, Great Britain and Ireland and the continent of Europe. It includes the printing of what we call literature in all the different languages of the countries in which we are undertaking to do business and indeed, in the immigration work in the United States we require to use printing in different languages, Scandinavan, German and French.
The expenditure in the fiscal year 1906-7 on this account was $117,500 for nine months.
Who gets up that literature, your own officers?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: We just do the best we can. Some of our own officers compile some of the publications and sometimes we engage the services of other parties.
How much have you paid for outside parties during the year and who were they?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The matter contained in the atlas of Canada, which has been distributed very extensively, was chiefly prepared by Mr. Carmen, of Montreal. He is a newspaper man employed on one of the papers there.
The ' Herald,' probably.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I think it is on the 'Star;' he is an editorial writer.
How many of these atlases were published last year?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: We have published several editions. I cannot give the actual figures, but approximately about 150,000.
What do they cost per copy?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The edition that is now being circulated costs 7i cents apiece in 100,000 lots. Another gentleman who was employed was a Mr. Cliff, a newspaper man of Sauit Ste. Marie, formerly resident in the Northwest for many years. Mr. Dean, editor of the Nelson * News,' contributed the matter for British Columbia that is contained in the atlas.
He tv as an unsuccessful candidate in the local election, was he not?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes.

In how many languages have they been published?
Mr. OLIVER, Seven languages. Mr. Kennedy, of the London ' Times ' staff, was engaged during the past winter to do some work, the results of which have only partly been published.
What would he know about Canada?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: He lived in Canada most of his life, being acquainted with conditions in Canada through his residence here for most of his adult life, and being in newspaper work and now resident in England, it was thought that he would be able to present Canadian facts in a manner that would appeal to the people of the British Islands possibly better than one who was not acquainted with the British Isles.
That would seem to be reasonable.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I was very much impressed with some work he did in describing the Northwest the year before in letters which appeared in the London ' Times,' and he afterwards practically compiled the same matter into a publication which he issued at his own cost in the old country.
I was very favourably impressed with his grasp of the subject and his method of presenting it, and went so far as to engage him especially to come to Canada during the past winter in order to present the conditions as to labour which existed then.
I suggested that by going through the maritime provinces he might prepare something in regard to those provinces in reference to which so far we have been rather lacking in literature.
Very neglectful of.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs

speechtext: I hope the minister has not neglected New Bfunswick?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: No, the matter which he has prepared for New Brunswick is in my hands, but I have not handed it to the printer, and lam expecting what he has to say about Prince Edward Island very shortly.
How much time did he spend in the maritime provinces getting up these facts?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I think about a month. Of course I must admit that the time is short. It seemed to me that this gentleman had particular ability in that line. We were doing the best we could to get the facts with regard to these provinces as well as we could gather them and present them in a form that would commend these provinces to the minds of the people in the old country for whom we think there is a desirable field there.

Some men could gather such information in a month and others would need six months, just depending upon the ability of the man. If Mr. Kennedy having had a long experience from residence in Canada is a clever man he ought to be able to present these facts in such a way as to be attractive to the English readers.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: That was my idea. [DOT] He is not a cheap man by any means.
It depends on his ability whether he is a cheap man or not. What will it cost?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I think the whole cost will be about $1,500 or $2,000.

What time will he occupy In that work?
Mr. FOWLER

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I can hardly say. It was an experiment and it appealed to me as being a good idea.	As we propose to
spend' a considerable sum of money in publications which will present these provinces to the people of the old country we think it is by no means waste to spend a good deal of money in getting the right matter.	.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: That is a sound principle because the printing and distribution will cost the same whether the matter is good or bad. I agree that it is worth while to try the work of a man who understands the view point of the people among whom the literature is to be distributed. I think the minister has made a wise move in that.
I suppose this literature is first written in English and translated into the various languages?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes.
What are the seven languages?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: English, French, German, Flemish, Holland (Dutch), Danish, Swedish, Norwegian and Finnish.
I see that the London ' Advertiser ' was paid for printing 50.000 copies of the land reports. In what form were they printed, and were they intended for distribution in eastern Canada?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: That particular pamphlet was intended for distribution especially in Great Britain.
Are the subagents resident in the United States working under our salaried agents at different points?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes.

Was any portion of this vote used for paying for these new Doukho-bors that have come to the country?
Mr. OLIVER, No. I presume my hon. friend refers to reports in the newspapers as to a carload of Doukhobors having some trouble with regard to their passage money.
I think it was a train load.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I can assure my hon. friend that so far as any information we have in the department goes no Doukhobors have come to this country, and if any have come they have certainly come without cost to the government and without any inducement being held out by the government in any shape or manner. We are informed that one family arrived about two months ago, but as they did not come within the requirements of our present regulations

which are somewhat stringent, they were excluded.
How long has the government ceased to encourage the immigration of Doukhobors?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I might answer that by saying seven years, but to make it plain I should say that the arrangement entered into with regard to the Doukhobors was a single effort in relation to a certain special colony or section, and was supposed to be made in the joint cause of religious liberty and the beneficial settlement of the Northwest. It was not carried any further.
How many of the Doukhobors migrated last year to British Columbia?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: We have no official information. Our immigration branch is not responsible in regard to the colony as now constituted. But I have heard through the ordinary channels that about 100 heads of families have recently gone to British Columbia to occupy lands which have been purchased there on behalf of the community.

I understood that an order had been issued by the department compelling the Doukhobors who desired to live in the communal condition to give up the lands that had been issued to them. Is that correct ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: That is hardly the way I would care to have the matter put. The Doukhobors made homestead entry for certain lands in 1903, but did not comply with the homestead conditions.
Were those entries made by the individuals themselves or by some person on behalf of them.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: They were made just as other entries were at that time allowed to be made, that is to say, they were proxy entries. Ostensibly they were made for the individual Doukhobors, each of whom made his entry in exactly the same terms as other people, and signed his application in just the same way.
Afterwards ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: No. The entrant was not required to be in bodily presence in the land office, but he had to sign his application personally and he became responsible for the affidavit contained in the application.
Was there not such a think as a blanket entry which the individual did not have to sign?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
No. When the Doukhobors came to the country certain lands were set apart as a service, upon which 316
they alone might secure homestead entry. Up to 1903 few if any of them had made entry. In 1903 they were informed by the department that if they were going to retain control of those lands, or any part of them, they must make entry for them. In accordance with the negotiations that then took place, they made entry in the way that I have mentioned, on the ordinary forms, and these forms were accepted, and their entries stood in the book against those lands subject to the ordinary homestead conditions.

What precaution (lid you take to make yourselves sure that the signature to the application was that of the individual, and that some one person did not sign 100 or perhaps 200 applications ? Did you have them witnessed or sworn to ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I do not think the affidavit requires witnesses.
The applicant has to swear that he is the person making the entry ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Yes, as I understand it. At any rate, the entries were made, and the people who made the entries, in the large majority of cases instead of breaking away from the community system, as had been expected, were rather more confirmed in the community system than before, and were not conforming to the terms of the entry, as the law required. The matter was under consideration for some time; but the upshot of it was that in the early part of 1907 a commission was appointed to visit the settlements and to find out how many of these people were conforming to the requirements of the Homestead Act. The Rev. John McDougall was the commissioner, with Mr. Mavor, a clerk in the employ of the lands branch of the Interior Department, and Michael White, a man of Russian birth and German parentage, who understood the Russian language and was educated in English, as interpreter. They examined the conditions carefully, and ascertained how many people were conforming to the terms of the Homestead Act and how many did not wish to conform, as nearly as they could. They made a calculation as to how much land would be required to give to those who did not want to conform to the terms of the Homestead Act, enough land to cultivate and occupy and make a living upon. It was found that during the seven years that the Doukhobors had been in the country, their total cultivation amounted to about five acres per head of men, women and children. Before we appointed this commission we had arrived at the conclusion that we could not and would not be



justified in maintaining their homestead entries against lands in regard to which the duties were not being fulfilled, and that if they refused to conform to the requirements of the law by individual ownership and cultivation, there was no recourse hut to cancel their entry and leave the lands open to entry and occupation by other persons. At the same time, we had to recognize that the people were there, and that they had been living from the products of their fields for some seven years-because I may say that, with the exception of the expenses iucurred in connection with their coming to the country and their first year's residence here, they have been no cost to the government in any shape or manner.
What was the cost of their first year's residence ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I cannot answer that. They were responsible for certain advances which were made, but I cannot say just how the account stands. But since then they have been entirely self-supporting, and not only that, but they have been reasonable contributors to the general productiveness and therefore the wealth of the country. We found that they would not conform to the requirements of the Homestead Act. Their religious belief absolutely precludes private ownership of anything particularly private ownership of land ; they abhor the idea.

That being the case, why did these people make these applications for the homesteads ? Either they must have been deceived when they made them or else they were false to their religion, or they have changed their views since.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I think it was a little of all three. When our commission visited them, they declared that their religious belief prohibited the private ownership of land. That was in the early part of 1907. They were then more than self-supporting. They were adding measurably to the production and wealth of the country, and we did not consider that we would be justified, although they were not conforming to the requirements of our homestead laws, in taking action which would amount to saying to them: You must get off the earth. We did not think we would he justified in doing so, as a matter of common humaftity. Those people had been then five or six years in the country, they had five acres per head under cultivation, they had been supporting themselves successfully and accumulating a little wealth off that area, and if we continued to their use say three times that much land, we thought they could have no possible grounds of complaint, and they would have abundance of opportunity for reasonable expansion as their population increased. Therefore around each Mr. OLIVER.
village we gave a reserve which would aggregate in area fifteen acres per head of the people resident in that village.
About seventy-five acres to a family.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Their families are small. They hardly average as large as those of the surrounding settlers. First we cancelled all the entries, we cleared the books of the entries made by the Doukhobors who were not conforming to the homestead conditions, and in the vicinity of each village, including the site, we held in reservation land aggregating fifteen acres to each resident for the benefit of that village. We said we would hold that in the hands of the Crown for their use and benefit, so long as they saw fit to use It and we saw fit to let them have it. That was not done by agreement but of our motion. The remainder of the land held under entry by them, saving that held in conformity with our homestead law [DOT]-because quite a considerable number did conform with the homestead law-was declared open for homestead entry. We announced in the newspapers that on June 1. 1907, there would be open for homestead entry to the first applicant at the counter the land thus cancelled in a certain township; that on the second day, the land in another township would be opened, and so on until all the land which had been cleared off the books had been offered to the public for homestead entry. All of the land has not been taken because some of it is not desirable. Still there was quite a rush for the land, and the great majority of it was taken up.
Odd as well as even-numbered sections?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: In the York district their reserve included the odd sections as well as the even. In the Prince Albert district, they only had the even sections. The odd-numbered sections were held for other settlement.	[DOT]
Who were associated with the Rev. John McDougall ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Mr. Maber of the Interior Department and Mr. White as interpreter.
About how long were they occupied?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: What my hon. friend is asking me now has to do with the lands branch, and the officials present are not able to give the information at the moment.

We can defer any discussion on that until those estimates come up. I observe that the Rev. John McDougall, was paid for services $3,910 and there was advanced him for expenses $4,600. When these estimates come up, I shall ask for further details.

Is that the same Rev. John McDougall, who figured in the newspapers a little while ago as speaking very eulogistically of this government? Perhaps that newspaper did not come to the attention of the minister. We shall perhaps be able to see some reason why the reverend gentleman should speak ofjhis government in such very high terms.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I am sure he had every reason to speak in the highest terms of this government and so would every other honest man.
He had nine thousand reasons-good crisp Dominion bank bills.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: That hardly applies to the subject before the House. I may say that this matter was not one to be easily approached. It was an undertaking of very considerable delicacy and difficulty. Now that it is over, it looks quite easy, but I beg to assure my hon. friend that I approached it with anything but confidence. However something had to be done, the question had to be dealt with, and I saw no better way to deal with it. Whatever my hon. friends may think of the amount paid the Rev. Mr. McDougall or the commission, my belief is that the money was well spent in getting a satifactory settlement of a difficult and delicate question, affecting a very large area of very valuable land.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: That is what I wanted to ask about. He cancelled their entries and gave them fifteen acres in the centre of the village for each person residing in the village. Did they thoroughly understand that and are they satisfied with it ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: That is my information. Of course, I cannot say that they were satisfied with it in the first place. Two deputations came dowm to interview me, objecting to the action we proposed to take. Although their religious views were entirely prohibitive of the private ownership of land, those views did not prohibit, apparently, the community ownership of land, and they were prepared to assert the retention of the control by the community over this area on which they seem to think they had some special claim as a community and were prepared to excite sympathy throughout the country and generally to make as strong a case as they possibly could. However, I think, owing very greatly to the tact of Mr. McDougall and his assistants on the commission, since the work was actually done, I have not heard one word of complaint either directly or indirectly from the Doukhobors or from the public except in isolated instances from people who felt, perhaps, that their particular right was not given the consideration they might have wished.	[DOT]
How many communities did Rev. John McDougall deal with and where are they located?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: If my memory serves me well, there were forty or forty-one villages. The majority-about thirty-were located in what is called the Yorkton district, that is, north of Yorkton and on the line of the Canadian Northern Railway. Some ten or twelve villages were situated in the Prince Albert district west of Rosthemr also on the Canadian Northern Railway. My hon. friend will understand that when the Doukhobors were located on these lands the lands were distant from railway communication and were not considered valuable to any degree. They were good enough for the Doukhobors, but not good enough for anybody else. But when the railroad was run through these tracts, the condition was absolutely changed. Besides there had been seven years' residence of the Doukhobors, during which time the fertility oif the soil and the suitability of the climate had been demonstrated. So when the road was constructed these lands acquired a very great value-not only an actual, but a speculative value. We had not only the difficulty of dealing with the Doukhobors, who thought they owned the land or ought to own it, but we had also the difficulty of dealing with the people who saw in it a very considerable cash value which they felt that they would like to handle, and thought it was theirs by right as citizens of the country who were first on the ground to get it.

I think the principal objection of the people in these respective localities was that the holding of these lands by the Doukhobors retarded development. I had occasion to travel across that country and know the most valuable lands in these districts that had been located upon. People of other 'nationalities who went there found that they could not carry [DOT] on their farming operations successfully in the same locality owing to the difference of habit and custom, and so they naturally asked the government to deal with the matter in -some way. Are all these districts dealt with ? Have all these questions been settled ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes.

Well, now that is over, perhaps the minister would say whether lie thinks that the system the government adopted by way of cancellation and reopening these homesteads was the best "way in the interests of the people ? The reason why I ask is that I know a good many people who went from Manitoba to that section to secure homesteads and who underwent a good deal of hardship-they had to wait day by day upon the officials wlio were dealing with these homesteads, and many, when they got to the place where they had to make application, had

to wait for hours in the rain before they could be admitted to the building where applications were to be filed. The Liberal press at that time gave great encouragement to all to go there and get a homestead, representing that all they had to do was to go there and there would be no difficulty. Consequently many went and spent a great deal of time and money, and underwent, as I have said, a great deal of hardship, and I think that about 80 per cent of them came away without being able to secure a homestead. This was due entirely to the manner in which the press of the country represented the facts at that time. There was quite a loss to people, some of them right in my own locality. I think the government might have adopted a different system. Even had the minister followed the system in vogue in the United States in opening up tracts of country, I think the results would have been better. It is all over now, but I do think that the government might have adopted a better system in throwing open these holdings.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I do not know that any important purpose will be served by discussing the matter now. But it appears that the only objection that the hon. gentleman (Mr. Staples) makes to the system adopted by the government to make these lands available is that it was too popular-too many people applied for homesteads. But I think that when we offered the land to the first comer, advertised the fact that it would be available to the first comer, and opened it up township after township so as to minimize the rush, we did as well as my hon. friend (Mr. Staples) could have done had he had to deal with the same conditions.

I did not pretend to suggest a policy. But I did refer him to the policy adopted in the United States, and I think that the people there get just as well satisfied as the men did who went out to get these homsteads.

The minister (Mr. Oliver) has spoken very highly of the services of the Rev. Mr. McDougall. But the minister's commendation, high as it is, is scarcely in proportion to the salary which the reverend gentleman receives for these services. I am sorry to differ in opinion from the minister, for very often I agree with him in the work of his department-and that is something that I cannot do with the heads of some of the departments-but I must say that I think these results could have been obtained just as well without the services of the Rev. Mr. McDougall. I think this result could have been obtained just as well without the services of the Rev. Mr. McDougall as with his services. It would appear to me that these people being of a peculiar religious faith, the introduction among them Mr. STAPLES.
of a gentleman who represented a different faith, would naturally antagonize them; and perhaps a layman would have had a far better chance of succeeding in allaying any suspicion or ill feeling they might have had,, than would a gentleman wearing the uniform of the church. As to the agreement that was made, as to the disposition that was made of these lands, I do not know that I have any fault to find with that at all. I think the government was generous with these people in allowing them to remain on this land that they had cultivated, perhaps not too generous. But I do think that the money that was expended in connection with this mission was absolutely thrown away. The same information could have been gathered by the inspectors which the hon. gentleman employed, and their reports should have been sufficient for him to act upon. His own officers could have reached the same result without any additional cost. This government is altogether too fond of issuing commissions in order to reward their political friends. We saw in the papers the other day that tiie Rev. Mr. McDougall had given this government a clean bill of health; there seemed to be a mutual service and the reverend gentleman was no doubt well recompensed for his services. It seems to me that these gentlemen must have lived at a pretty expensive rate, since the expenses amounted to close upon $5,000 for the party. In the party there were only three persons. Mr. McDougall himself, Mr. Michael White, the interpreter, and Mr. Major, the officer of the department. Their expenses amounted to $4,600. I suppose it was thought prudent to travel in a magnificent style so as to impress the Doukho-bors and to make them think that this new religious leader occupied as high a position as Mr. Peter Verigen did in the minds of the Doukhobors. As regards the land settlement, I think the minister acted properly. If these people choose not to conform to the regulations of the land department, it was right to take the lands from them; and again, having come under the conditions which they did, and being in the country, it was necessary to do something with them, and perhaps the minister took the wisest course in allowing them the 15 acres per head. Have these Doukhobors votes?-because it would look as if the government thought that would be a nice way to obtain control of the votes of these communities.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
No, they object just as strongly to becoming citizens as they do to owning land. To return to the items of expenditure, we are estimating for British bonuses this year, $90,000. In the year 1906-7 we paid $58,000 on that account for nine months. That goes to the booking agent's in Great Britain and Ireland. We have not got the figures for the year since

the 31st of March last. But we are asking $90,000 for the current year.
How many individuals are there to whom this $58,000 was paid?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: There are about 1,800 hooking agents entitled to the bonus. We have a printed list of the names. We estimate $10,000 for continental bonuses, that is, bonuses on immigrants from continental Europe. We give bonuses on the same classes as we do in Great Britain, that is, people who have followed agriculture, and who intend to follow it in this country. During the fiscal year, 1906-7, there were no bonuses paid except those paid in winding up the business of the North Atlantic Trading Gompany. As I have informed the House, we closed business with that company on the 30th November, 1906, and we did not begin to pay bonuses on any other account until some time in 1907. The bonuses which we were entitled to pay in the early part of 1907 had not accrued until the close of that fiscal year, therefore there is nothing shown as having been paid in bonuses during that fiscal year except those paid to the North Atlantic Trading Company, which were earned before the 30th November, 1906.
They have not earned anything since you cut them off?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: No, but they say they have.

Are they suing you ? In that case we will get their names.
keeping track of the number he sends is his weekly report of the reduced-fare tickets which he issues by authority of the railway companies.
Would that be a good test ? Would it not be possible for people simply coming to visit their relatives in Canada to get these tickets ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:

speechtext: A few moments ago I received a telegram concerning this Bill. I have no information on the subject other than that contained in the telegram which is addressed to me from Montreal and which is as follows :

A shareholder of Crown Life.
My hon. friend from Norfolk (Mr. Tisdale) is familiar with the matter and I call his attention to this. I have no other knowledge than that which comes by this telegram.

Every shareholder had notice at least three or four weeks ago before the Bill was introduced in the Senate. In the (Standing Orders Committee there was an affidavit filed that every one of them had notice in addition to the public notices which have now run their full time, that this Act would be applied for at this session. Sir. Roberts, the gentleman who sent that telegram, was formerly connected with the company, but we found it necessary to dispense with his services three or four years ago, and he has since been trying to give us all possible annoyance. The Bill is important to us as an enabling Bill, and therefore I wish to press it. We have to get a two-thirds votes of the proprietors before we can do anything under the Act, and it is most important, in the interests of the company, that we should have a chance of bringing the matter before the shareholders and getting it settled.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I would suggest, in view of what the hon. member for Norfolk has said, that we let the Bill go through its present stage, and stand for a third reading. The telegram does not come from him, but from Mr. Roberts. It is most important in the interest of the company that we should get the Bill through so that if bills are assented to next week, we may save a month or six weeks in the reorganization. I may say that I represent now considerably more than half the proxies, apart from those shareholders who have not yet sent in their answers. A notice of what we were doing was sent to every shareholder. If we have any trouble, let us settle it before the shareholders. speechtext: Yes.

At six o'clock the hon. minister made the remark, if I caught his words correctly, that the American immigrants to the Northwest were a good class of immigrants notwithstanding the evidence from this side of the House. I do not know what evidence the minister refers to.
I wish to state here that the class of American immigrants we are getting in Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta is a very desirable class. They are men of experience who come with considerable money and they have shown their ability to get to work and develop that western country. When the minister says there is evidence from, this side that we consider them not desirable, I cannot agree with him. I am sure I have not heard any one on this side reflect in any way on those immigrants. Where he got that evidence I would like to know. It would be well for this government to expend a large amount of their appropriations set aside for importing immigrants from the continent and devote it to bringing in the class of American immigrants we are getting. Take the large amount of money given the North Atlantic
