Trading Company and other companies of that nature in return for which this country has received little or no benefit and a very poor class of immigrants as compared with the Americans.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I am sure the hon. gentleman's expression of opinion as regards the American immigrants is acceptable to all ex-members of this House.
I notice in the Auditor General's Report, L-23, a list of special delegates. What are they for?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: A considerable proportion of those are practical farmers who are selected and sent to the old country because of the success they have achieved in Canada. We prefer to send delegates to the old country who have been born there and who have made a success in Canadian farming. These men are paid $100 a month and their expenses. While in the British Isles they are under the direction and control of our immigration service there and are generally employed in visiting the offices of the foreign booking agents. The booking agent makes the announcement that on a certain day a certain farmer from Canada will be at his office and be glad to meet any one who desires information regarding Canada. These men are not generally public speakers, but practical, successful men. And when given the opportunity of meeting practical men in the same business, they put the advantages of Canada in a very direct and favourable light.
Where do you send them ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
They all report at our head office in London and then the assistant commissioner distributes them according to his best judgment and the localities from which they may come originally, and according also to the energy or reliability of the various booking agents. There may be a booking agent in a certain locality who does not take an active interest in his business, and it would not be worth while sending a delegate to him, and there may be another in a farming locality who may be very active.
Mr. FOWrLER. Are they only sent to the British Isles?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes, but last year we sent a Frenchman to France and a Belgian to Belgium.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I cannot say, but $100 is the maximum. No doubt there was an arrangement with Mr. Shepherd, and he was satisfied with the amount paid him. We desire to get men who have a going business and cannot leave without paying others to take their place, and we pay them sufficient to enable them to engage substitutes.

Mr. Shepherd is one of our best farmers, and he had to leave some one in his place. I heard indirectly that he felt somewhat annoyed on learning that the expense account lie put in and the salary he asked had been pared down to a certain extent. He is just as good a man as the government could send from their side of politics. Why he should not receive as much salary as Mr. Larkin and many others, I do not know.

speakerposition: Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Are they all Liberals?
As far as I know they are, and should be treated equally.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I really cannot say why Mr. Shepherd was not paid as much as the others, or why his expense account was not as great. I suppose that the fact that he was not paid so much is not an objection to the amount he was paid. At any rate we cannot be charged with extravagance in the case of Mr. Shepherd.

When Mr. Shepherd was in Europe, he did good service to the coun-tw Ho paid careful attention to the way our grain "reached the foreign market. He brought home samples and exhibited them in the Agricultural Committee. I do not see why he should not receive every consideration at the hands of the government.

In this list of special delegates, I see a familiar name-Wagner. This delegate is named M. Wagner. Would that be a relative of Philip of that ilk .
Mr m\rvETt. Not that I am aware of.

Where did M. Wagner go*to!_to Great Britain or to the continent ? I see the amount is stated here as an ' advance ' on his travelling expenses. He got his ocean passage of $30 and an advance of $75 How much salary was paid to M..- which might stand for Michael ; we will call him Michael-Wagner, and what expenses did he receive besides this advance of $75 ?

I see in the Auditor General's Report, page L-24, that Mr. Larkin, one of those delegates, received $100 a month and $200 expenses. Another delegate, Mr. A. Shepherd, who is quite a capable man, just as capable as Mr. Larkin, only received $75 a month and $70.30 expenses. Why this discrimination?
I am not able to answer ie question. He was to have his passage aid and lie received an advance on expenis. But his accounts were not reeeivea onttlement when the books were closed.
Is he in the employ of the government ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Evidently, he is one of the delegates sent to the old country-I fancy to Germany, judging by the name.

I see here also Rev. Mr. Woodcutter, salary four months at $83.33, ocean passages $59.20, and travelling expenses $678.73. How does it come that the Rev. Mr. Woodcutter has such a large bill for expenses, and was paid salary for four months while most of the others were paid for from one to three months ? Was Mr. Woodcutter a farmer ? Or how and why was he sent ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: His calling is indicated by his title-he is a Roman Catholic clergyman. He is a man of very wide linguistic accomplishments, speaking a number of European languages. He was for a time in our employment at the Winnipeg office as an interpreter. Some time after his continuous employment at the immigration hall Winnipeg had ceased, it was his desire to visit Continental Europe, and we thought we should be well-advised to put him on the same footing as a farmer delegate, though he is not a farmer.

In fact, to give him an outing in Europe, you appointed him a special farming delegate, paid him for four months, gave him $59.20 for ocean passage -double what you gave anybody else-and paid him $678.73 for his expenses.

Has the minister had any recent complaint from the south, of agents recommending people to go to any particular section of the country ? There were complaints about a year ago from Macleod and that section, of agents somewhere in the United States recommending settlers going into Canada to go to the northern and not to the southern part, on the ground that the south was a poor place for settlers to locate.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: No complaints have come to my knowledge within the past year. As my hon. friend (Mr. Herron) has said, there were complaints about a year ago. I am bound to say that, on inquiry, I did not find that those complaints were well founded.
Can the minister tell me the cost of maintenance of the office in London, England ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The Auditor General's Report shows that for the nine months ending March 31, 1907, the amount was $26,463.76. Adding one-fourth, you get a very close approximation to the amount we are asking parliament for.
McCarthy. How many are employed on the staff in that office ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: There are thirteen employees.

McCarthy. I do not know whether it has come to the attention of the minister or not, but the management of that office has been the subject of certain criticism in the. western newspapers. I have seen a number of articles in newspapers published in Alberta, one purporting to give an interview with a gentleman who had recently visited the London office. This gentleman said that he tried to get some information there regarding the province of Alberta. He was handed two pamphlets six years old and could get practically no attention or information about the country. Without taking time to read these statements, I should be glad to send the papers to the minister if he has not seen them.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I have seen papers which I have no doubt are the ones to which the hon. gentleman alludes. One statement is made by Captain Thomas, of Camrose, and the other by Mr. Blaylock, of Calgary. I referred these statements to the office in London for explanation. I have not received the explanation as yet. I hope that the conditions are not quite correctly represented. But if they are, certainly some rearrangement requires to be made. When I was in that office myself it seemed to me that matters were being handled in a very different manner and a different spirit. We have supplied what we thought was up to date literature. It may be that our supply of up to date literature had at that particular moment been exhausted. We supply literature from this side, and it is possible that the new supply had not arrived at the time this gentleman called. I think there must be some explanation such as that.

The statement of Mr. Blaylock was that he could get no information about the southern part of the province, and all he could find in the offices was a bird's eye view of the city of Edmonton. If what he states is true, while the people of southern Alberta have no objection to Edmonton being advertised in the London office as much as the minister chooses, they do not think the advertisement should be confined to that part of Alberta and that particular city.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I think the House will see that the two witnesses who have been called by my hon. friend for the prosecution hardly agree. One gentleman complains that he could not get anything up-to-date relating to Alberta and the other gentleman complains because he did get that 'which was up-to-date and which related to Alberta, because it did not relate to southern Alberta.
8. McCarthy. What did he get that w-as up-to-date ?

speakerposition: subtopic
Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
A view of Edmonton, as he says. If the description he did receive at the immigration office was a little out of the actual facts, the complaint of Capt. Thomas was that the information was too far out of date. In regard to the statement of Mr. Blaylock, I think I saw some discussion in the newspapers about it, and my opinion would be that some enterprising people of Edmonton had sent to the London office some advertising matter on their own account, and that Mr. Blaylock had seen it there. If the people of Calgary chose to send anything advertising their city it would receive the same prominence.
I want to assure the House that none of the publications sent out by this department, place Edmonton in the light that my hon. friend speaks of, as compared with any other city in Alberta or in Canada.

McCarthy. I asked the minister if he had seen these complaints, and from what he has said I believe now that he has seen them. Having seen them,
I would ask him to investigate them and see if they are well founded.

I notice in the Auditor General's Report the sum of $92,614 paid for bonuses. This, I presume, is the sum the details of which are given on L-24 and 25, for bringing immigrants to this country. On L-23 is a sum of $19,725 under head of grants made to various corporations and associations. Would the minister give some explanation of this latter sum, and state why those grants were made ? They are apparently made to associations connected with immigration, and are expended in part at least upon immigrants after they reach Canada. How does that explanation fit with the grant of $6,000, for instance, to the Quebec and Lake St. John Railway Company ? I notice that nearly $20,000 goes to associations in the province of Quebec. I understand that Quebec was in the same position as Ontario with regard to immigration agents, who are paid for the location of immigrants in that province. For what reason is the grant of this very large sum made to associations, and in what way would the Quebec and Lake St. John Railway get their grant ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I am glad my hon. friend ' has asked this question. We have had several attempts made in the House, both this session and the previous session, to make it appear that there was some undue discrimination by the immigration department in respect to securing and distributing settlers. The Department of Immigration is interested in securing desirable people to settle in all parts of the Dominion, its efforts and its expenditures are directed in the first place, to inducing the settler
to come, and in the next place, to establishing him in the country to the best advantage. The one great difference between the policy of the present government and that of the late government, was that the late government rather confined its efforts to inducing people to come, and did not proceed further to help them to establish themselves in the various parts of the country. This government has adopted the policy of endeavouring to secure the establishment of the settler in the country after his arrival. It is for that reason that our immigration staff in Winnipeg is so large. We have a commissioner of immigration at Winnipeg, with a large and expensive staff, an immigration hall with a great many appurtenances of different kinds. We have immigration agents and immigration halls at many other points throughout that country, and land guides at many points. All this vast expenditure is made for the purpose of locating the settler where he desires to settle after he has reached Canada. In the province of Ontario we have taken an interest in placing immigrants by establishing employment agencies in the different counties. The agents work on a commission basis, and receive $2 for each immigrant that they place on a farm in the;7' respective counties.

That policy it seems to me has resulted in the appointment as employment agents of partisan supporters of the government who work almost solely for the $2 a head, and the system does not seem to me to be very successful. If people of a higher standard were employed, such as we had formerly in my own county, I think the results would be very different. The results from that system in the county which I have the honour to represent have certainly up to the present been anything but satisfactory.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I was not for the moment discussing that side of the question.
I was saying that we were making certain efforts in Ontario as well as in the west to place immigrants satisfactorily after their arrival. The expenditure my hon. friend has quoted from the Auditor General's Report as being made in Quebec are for the same purpose and to the same end. They are made on a different method from that employed in Ontario, just as the method in Ontario is different from the method in the prairie west.
Are there any employment agents in Quebec paid in the same way?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Yes, but that is a very recent development and, in fact, can scarce-lv be considered to be an effective measure as yet, because, as my hon. friend knows, a large part of the population of Quebec is of the French language, and unless there

are French immigrants who come and are available to be placed, there is very little of that to be done. There has been little placing of immigrants in actual practice as yet in Quebec except in the English counties. We have made expenditures in Quebec with a view to having the immigrants whom we induced to come to the country satisfactorily placed in the positions which would be of advantage to them and to the country. The payment to the Lake St. John Railway is one of these payments. The ' Lake St. John Railway is a colonization railway. It gives communication with points reached by it in the Lake St. John region where there is some agricultural development and where there is industrial development of various kinds. It seemed reasonable that the Lake St. John Railway, being especially interested in the colonization and development of that country, should be considered and dealt with as an active and effective agent for handling and dealing with people desirous of going into that country. There are several societies in the province of Quebec looking to the development of the hinterland of that province, and we have made certain payments to these societies with the same object of having the immigrant on his arrival placed satisfactorily so that both he and the country will be benefited. The payments in Quebec are for the same purposes as in Ontario and the west, hut they are made on a different principle because of the different condition of the country.
In what way do the Lake St John Railway do the work?. Do they place immigrants on their own land or how do they distribute them and find them employment?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The railway company have no grant of land. The unoccupied land in that locality is owned by the provincial government. In consideration of this grant the railway company gives free transportation from Quebec over their railway.
Are these French immigrants who are brought in there?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Some are French, but there are some Belgians and other nationalities as well. Of course, it is natural that a settlement in that province will attract French immigrants, but the settlement is not confined to French. There is a Danish as well as a Belgian settlement there.
Do the society of colonization and repatriation and the Quebec and Lake St. John Colonization Society deal with the same section of country?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: In the estimates of the current year we are not asking ifor any money for the Lake St. John Colonization Society. We now confine our grants to the Railway.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs

speechtext: Is this grant of $300 the only grant to the Salvation Army in connection with the work ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: No, that is not the only grant the Salvation Army get. That grant is paid in the year mentioned, but it relates to services given in a previous year. It provides for the special lectures given under the auspices of the Army, very much as the meetings I have described are held by ordinary booking agents employing farm delegates.
That would be for services rendered in Europe?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: In England.
It is here under the head of grants.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: But the service is rendered in Great Britain.
What other grants are made to the Salvation Army as a body in Canada with reference to immigration work ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: We are paying the Salvation Army a special grant this year in consideration of their placing immigrants in the four western provinces. The Salvation Army sees to the placing of their immigrants after their arrival in this country. They have a very complete and successful organization, and as they have recently developed their work very largely in the west we have thought it not inadvisable to recognize their services to the extent I have mentioned. West of Lake Superior we have our own staff on salary to look after the placing of immigrants and we do not pay a commission per head as in Ontario. The Salvation Army also has its staff and we pay it a lump sum of $7,500 for the work done in the four western provinces.

Has the department an agent at Quebec who exchanges foreign money into Canadian money for the immigrants?
Mr. OLIVER, We have an arrangement with James MacNider & Co., brokers of Quebec, to exchange the money of the immigrants, and we pay MacNider & Co. $250 a year, and give them an office in the immigrant building.
And furniture ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The furniture is very limited.
What arrangement is made for that service in the winter?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: We have a similar arrangement at St. John with J. M. Robinson.

I have had correspondence from some persons in connection with this matter and they are under the impres-

sion that the profit on the exchange is more than the government grant. Other people are willing to do the work without any grant.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Perhaps so. It is very important that this exchange of money should be done by people who can absolutely be depended upon whether it pays them or not. It may be that the business has increased to such an extent that there is a profit in it without any payment by the government. But I presume the payment was made when the business was less extensive and when there was no profit in the exchange itself. We handle a great many immigrants at Quebec and if we can get a competent and reliable person to do his work it is cheap at $250 a year.
Has the government any information as to what the profits on the exchange are?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: No.
Has the exchange agent an absolutely free hand, or is there any oversight on him?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: He is bound to give the bank rate of exchange. He is there under the eye of the officials and subject to any complaints that may be made.
He is dealing with a class who are not very likely to know the bank rate of exchange.

Has the minister any information as to the character of the immigrants brought out by the Salvation Army ? The Army officers claim they have brought out suitable immigrants and that none of them have become a public charge, whereas others declare that the immigrants are of an inferior class and not suitable to the requirements of our country. Have any of the Salvation Army immigrants been deported?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Considering the large number of people who have come out under the auspices of the Salvation Army the failures are very few. There have been instances where some have had to be deported, and there are some others in which the immigrants might be considered undesirable, but considering that thousands have been brought out by the Army it is safe to say that generally speaking the Army immigrants are perfectly desirable. We have had practically no complaint with regard to these immigrants. We find the army a reliable institution who take care of the people they bring out, and if they find they have made a mistake they are as ready to rectify it as we could expect them to be.

I quite believe that the Salvation Army looks carefully after the immigrants brought out under their auspices. I understand, however,
they do not confine their efforts to the agricultural class and domestic servants for whom we pay the bonus. The Salvation Army take a proportion of their immigrants from the cities so that the government in paying them a lump sum is paying for a class of immigrants other than those specified in the order in council.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: It is possible to place such construction upon the grant, but after all it is hardly fair because there is no doubt this Salvation Army brings out a very large proportion of agricultural people. It is true that they do not confine their efforts to that class, although we confine our bonus to that class; but the grant we have under discussion now is paid to them ^ in respect of the work they do in distributing their immigrants west of Lake Superior, and I think, everything considered, they are entitled to the amount we pay them for that service, although it is not distinguished in the account from the other branches of their service. So that my hon. friend may claim, if he pleases, that we are indirectly assisting in bringing out people other than the agricultural class. We think that we may claim in fairness that we are not.
Is that the only organization or society to which the government gives a grant for the purpose of assisting in the work of bringing immigrants from "the old country?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Allow me to put it the other' way. We are not paying them this money to assist them in bringing people out. We are paying them to assist them in distributing the immigrants after they have come out. We are not paying a similar grant to any other society, because so far as I know there is no other society that distributes the immigrants it brings out.
I notice that you employ a number of clergymen. In the Auditor General's Report is a statement of the expense of employing four clergymen. What are their duties?	[DOT]

The principle on which thev are employed is pretty much the same as 'that on which the importunate widow secured her desire. There are times and occasions (When it is very difficult to do otherwise than accede to the propositions that are made. As I have already said, our principle is to employ practical farmers, but we are not always able to secure the' men we want of that class.

What are these clergymen employed for? They do not understand farming. What pressure did they put on the department to cause themselves to be employed? I do not think the widow story will exactly cover the ground. Is it because they wish to take a trip abroad

for the purpose of their health? There ought to he some reason given for this employment other than the fact that they belong to the clerical profession.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The reasons which they give, and which may very well be given, are that having lived most of their lives in country districts and in close touch with agricultural operations, they have a very good knowledge of practical farming; and of course, being accustomed to public speaking, they have ability in the way of addressing audiences that ordinary practical farmer may not have. While we do not object to utilizing the services of the clergymen or think lightly of their services, we want to confine our operations as closely as possible to the strictly agricultural class. Therefore, as like attracts like, we expect best to attract that class of people by sending as delegates successful actual farmers, and we employ very few clergymen, as my hon. friend will see.

I notice that you have employed a doctor-Dr. Page, who visited Liverpool, Glasgow, London, Antwerp and Paris, for which he charged $439 for expenses in addition to his ocean passage ; and you also employed a Dr. Robins. What do you want doctors for ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Dr. Page is the examining officer at Quebec. He was sent to Europe for the purpose of better informing himself in regard to the sanitary conditions surrounding the emigrants and the diseases by which they are most likely to be affected; He was sent to Europe for the purpose of enabling him to give us better service at Quebec.

That is, you sent him to Europe to complete his education. I should have thought that he could have got sufficient practice by examining the people affected by trachoma and other diseases tvho come here. I notice that you sent two agents to Iceland. Why do you send two to that small island?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: We only send one each year, but the two names appear because of the overlapping of the account.
Do you keep a resident agent in Iceland?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: No. There are large and successful Icelandic settlements in Manitoba, and we send an agent from one of these each year for a period of about six months.
I notice that you paid the Allan Line bonuses on Icelandic settlers. Why do you do that? The Allan Line does not call at any Icelandic port.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: This is an exceptional transaction which pertains only to Iceland. It is a small country, with a small popula-1

tion, it is not on the ordinary lines of travel and the expense of immigrants coming from Iceland is much greater in proportion to the distance than those of immigrants from almost any other country. They have to make a trip from Iceland to some point in the British islands; they usually come by Leith. Instead of paying a booking agent $5 a head in this case, we have an arrangement whereby the steamship company reduces the fare to the passenger by the amount of $5 and we pay the steamship company. This is the only case in which we bonus the steamship company. In all other cases we bonus the booking agent as an encouragement to his publicity campaign on behalf of Canada. In the case of Iceland, the population is entirely agricultural or outdoor people. There are practically no undesirables in Iceland. Therefore we have made a special arrangement in their case.
Then this is partially assisted immigration ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes, but that is the only case.
Who pays the expense of sending a deported immigrant back ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The steamship company.

How is it then that we pay so much to these steamship companies for bringing them back ?
Mr. OLIVER, The railway and steamship companies have to bear the expense, provided the immigrant is deported within the year. But if he has been here more than a year, the steamship company returns him at a special rate called the charity rate. There are also cases in which it is impossible to locate the steamship company by which the undesirable immigrant came, and in such cases we pay the charity rate.
Do you not deport the undesirables from the points of debarkation such as Halifax, Quebec and Montreal? Why then all these charges t

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
If an immigrant does not pass the examination at the port where he lands, the steamship company has to take him back at once free of charge. But if he passes the examination and gets into the country and then we find he is an undesirable, we have to pay the costs of transportating him to the sea-board. Then if we can determine by what line he came and he is deported within the year, the company must carry him free. Otherwise we pay the charity rate.
Mr. FOWLER, I notice on page L-26 that 15,000 copies of the Halifax Chronicle,' a Dominion Exhibition number, were paid for at seven cents each or $1,132.50. What was that for ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: That was a number of the paper descriptive of Nova Scotia, its advantages and resources, and as we had not at that time published any literature having special reference to Nova Scotia, we thought it was not improper to Purchase a portion of this issue and distribute it in the British Isles.

Is that the issue of which some ten tons still remain over in the immigration office in London, much to the annoyance and inconvenience of the officers in charge ? There was something in the press to that effect.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I am afraid the report my hon. friend has mentioned must have appeared in the ' Halifax Herald.' I have no knowledge of there being any portion of this issue left on the hands of the department in London, and while I have heard many peculiar stories of the unadaptability of people on the other side, I would think that where there are so many opportunities of giving away these numbers, they would not be allowed to remain in the immigration office to the disadvantage of its business.
Has the immigration from the western states increased or decreased from latest reports ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Last year for many reasons it fell off considerably. This year the increase so far is very satisfactory over last year, but I do not think we have arrived at the volume of immigration of the year before, which was abnormal.

My hon. friend should encourage that immigration because it furnishes us with a very desirable class of settlers, From my observation and experience of these people, they are the best adapted to our western country. It makes no difference from what part of Europe they may originally have come to the United States, they have gained an experience In the western states which is of great advantage to them in our new country. No matter where you find American settlers, you find them adapting themseves to new conditions very much better than immigrants from elsewhere.

I notice that Mr. Ayotte is employed as an immigration agent in Montana and has received from this government $1,690 for the last nine months ending the 31st of March. What are his qualifications and what does he do ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
His headquarters are at Great Falls, Montana. He ,is working in the country in which my hon. friend from Alberta (Mr. Herron) has expressed a desire that we should, at any rate, not slacken
our efforts. I believe that Mr. Ayotte is originally from Manitoba.
What qualifications has he in education and ability ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I can hardly answer that question. I fancy by the results which we have from Montana, partly through the efforts of Mr. Ayotte and partly through the efforts of others, that he has the necessary qualifications.

He is a graduate of that notorious class of the Dominion elections of 1904, the Leach class. There were Leach, Ayotte, Ingram and Kneeham, all of whom did great work in disfranchising the electors of Manitoba. And every one of these men, very shortly after the elections, was taken charge of by the government and given a salary, so that they 'each of them' is drawing from the government from $1,200 to $4,000 a year. It is evident that Leach was the principal director and tutor of the class, for he is given the largest salary. According to the Auditor General's Report, he draws somewhere in the neighbourhood of $4,000. I am of opinion-and I think members of the House generally will agree with me-that these men were well rewarded for their great work in the elections of 1904.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: If this gentleman has done so much in disfranchising the Conservative electors of Manitoba, I fancy the hon. gentleman (Mr. Staples) will be well satisfied to have him located in Montana, and will consider it cheap at the price when we pay him a salary of only $900 a year.
Will the minister bring down the papers I asked for as to the distribution of provisions in Gimli?

While the minister is looking for these papers, I would draw his attention to another of the class referred to by my hon. friend from Macdonald (Mr. Staples), and even more successful in that particular line of work-W. T. It. Preston. I would refer the hon. minister to page L-23 of the Auditor General's Report, where he will find it stated that Mr. Preston was paid $1,127. Where is Mr. Preston now, if in the employ of the government, what is his title and what are his duties ? And can the minister say what success he has in the performance of those duties ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Preston is not in the employ of the Department of the Interior, so I am hardly in a position to give the hon. gentleman (Mr. Alcorn) the Information he desires. I understand, from reports which are as open to my hon. friend as to myself, that Mr. Preston is in the employ of the Department of Trade and Commerce as a commercial agent on the Asiatic coast of the Pacific. He was quite recently in Ja-

pan, but the latest I have heard in regard to him was that he was in either Corea or China, making a trip in the interests of Canadian trade. While not able to answer with authority, the information X have is that Mr. Preston has done good work in the promotion of Canadian trade with China, Corea and Japan.

I have seen in the newspapers statements somewhat similar to those made by the minister, but I was in hopes that the minister would be able to tell us precisely what Mr. Preston was doing for the large salary he commands at the hands of this government.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: He must be in Corea. I see the Japanese have sent a large army there.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I have here the file covering the report asked for by my hon. friend from Marquette (Mr. Roche). I will send it to him, but I would ask him not to consider it as a return laid on the table of the House, because I desire to keep it on the file in the department. I would like, however, to read the report of Mr. Walker made when his attention was drawn to the extract from the Selkirk 'Herald,' which my hon. friend read here last night. Under date of May 16, he says :
With reference to the inclosed extract from the Selkirk ' Record ' of April 25, in which it is implied, if not actually expressed that the Immigration Department has provided relief to settlers at Gimli, with a view of influencing these people politically.
I beg to say in reply that I am entirely responsible for the relief sent to the Galicians and other foreign settlers in the Gimli district, in townships 18, 19 and 20, ranges 2 and 3 east. That I have not been influenced in the slightest degree by any political circumstances, that as a matter of fact, I have no knowledge of the political leanings of the persons referred to, nor do I even know the name of the member of parliament, nor the political complexion of the member of parliament, who represents that district. Such action as I have taken has been done solely in the interests of humanity and in the interests of the successful settlement of that district. It seems to me to be extremely unkind, as I know it is altogether untrue, to add to the sufferings of these unfortunate people, by an accusation of seeking or obtaining help of this character without good reason.
I inclose herewith copies of correspondence relating to this relief, from which you will observe:
That a deputation of people petitioned the local land agent of the district for urgent help.
That the people so petitioning were not speaking for themselves, but for their neighbours, whom they described as almost starving.
That a deputation of these people, aided in their transportation by the railway company, appeared at my office, and appealed personally

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
for succor for their starving wives and children.
That John Lusted, a forest ranger, who lives in the locality, of his own initiative, wrote on the 12th March, among other things: ' There is a great destitution and almost starvation amongst the foreign settlers in that locality ' and ' I have found places where people are almost on the verge of starvation, having been two or three days without bread or flour to bake it-immediate relief is necessary/
That upon such urgent representations as this, I ordered on March 6 (see letter No. 1) Officer Abrahamson to proceed to the seat of the destitution, examine the matter carefully and closely, and report without delay.
On March 11 (see letter No. 2) I wrote Officer Abrahamson to remain and give his personal attention to this relief business. To investigate personally, each and every case, to report on each and every case and see that relief was given only to the most needy ones.
I inclose copy of his letter to me (see letter 3) in which he informs me that destitution of a severe character prevailed, not only among those whom he was sent to relieve, but others were coming and begging to him with the same cry for help.
On the 14th March I reported the circumstances to you (letter 4 herewith, being copy of my communication).
The shocking condition of destitution, verging upon absolute starvation, I found extended to altogether about 138 families in that neighbourhood.
In order to overtake the work satisfactorily, inquiring most rigidly into the merits of each case and to see that personal inspection was made before relief was given, I sent Officer Harvey to assist in the work.
In order further to satisfy myself that the needs of these people were really as serious as my information seemed to convey, I specially despatched Assistant Commissioner Gel-ley to look over the ground. He verified the reports of my officers, and to assist me in determining the amount and character of the assistance required. Assistant Commissioner Gelley fully bore out and confirmed the report of destitution.
I inclose herewith copy of the.joint report of Officers Abrahamson and Harvey as to the work they have done, the number of cases relieved and the character of the relief given. In addition to this, 85 families in the same neighbourhood required assistance. Some of those helped were Swedish arid other German settlers. I inclose copy of report by Officer Abrahamson on this last distribution.
In this very necessary work of distribution no help was given excepting what was urgently needed; no help was given excepting what was earnestly asked for; no help was given where the officers had not already satisfied themselves that it was necessary, and no help was offered any one who refused it. Liens were taken in the usual way, and only necessaries, such as flour, sugar and a little tea or coffee were given in anv case.
It is regrettable that the crop conditions of last year should have placed these people in such an unfortunate and unenviable position, and it is equally regrettable that irresponsible writers, for what purpose I do not know, should seek to throw discredit upon efforts

made to relieve their very serious and destitute condition.
Were these amongst the new arrivals?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Of that year and of the preceding year, that is to say, they were people who had come out and settled in a new country, and had not been able to get themselves well established before the bad season put them out of business so to speak.
Was assistance given to any but homesteaders?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: No.

On page L-14 of the Auditor General's Report, under the heading, ' Superintendent's Office, Ottawa,' I notice that a number of men are apparently employed by the department at $4 a day and their travelling expenses. For instance:
H. Charlebois, 103 days at $4; hoard and lodging, $227; pullman, $124; bus fares, $8; livery, $3; total, $741.70.
J.	O. Cowan, 102 days at $4; board and lodging, $264; pullman, $80; car fares, $4.80; care and board of immigrants, $7.50; telegrams, 50 cents; total, $649.75.
K.	J. Henry, board and lodgings and horse feed, $204.35; boat fares and meals, $7.10; cabs and livery, $347.75; railway and boat fares, $16.45; sleepers and parlour car, $25.65; small items, $1.07; total, $716.62.
G. A. Johnston, 91 days at $4; board and lodgings, $262.60; sleepers and parlour car, $119; street car and cabs, $4.75; telegrams, $1.25; total, $733.60.
What work were these men engaged in, and how did they come to expend these large sums in travelling expenses?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Some of the names mentioned by the hon. gentlemen are of men who were employed in accompanying immigrant trains from Ottawa to Winnipeg. It was thought advisable that a government officer should be on board the train to look after the immigrants and to see that things were kept right. At present we do not employ any one in that service. These men were employed by the trip and paid by the day, going and returning, and given their expenses. Mr. Henry is an inspector of immigrant children. We have an arrangement with the British government whereby there is an inspection of children sent out under the auspices of boards of guardians. When they come out to Can ada they are placed with farmers who desire to have them, and they are inspected yearly at the expense of the British government. We employ the inspector and pay him, and the British government recoup to us the expenditure.

Are these men constantly in the employ of the government, or are
they engaged to make these special trips only?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The inspectors of immigrant children are employed by the year, but the men who were employed on the train whose names the hon. gentleman read, were only employed by the trip.
What was the necessity for their returning in Pullman cars?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: In going to Winnipeg they travelled with the immigrants, and on their return there seems to be no reason why they should not travel comfortably.
They seem to have charged more for travelling than an ordinary traveller who pays his own way.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: We are not now employing men in that service.
Did these men produce vouchers for their expenses, those who travelled in parlour ears, or did the government pay the bill of every man as he put it in?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
They were required to produce vouchers.
Winnipeg and St. Boniface hospitals, $8,000.

I think that item is one that might be increased. There is no doubt that the hospitals in the city of Winnipeg are taxed heavily by the class of immigrants that are coining to this country. They are people with small means, and if they fall sick when they get here, they have to be placed in a hospital and well cared for. During the first session of this parliament I read to this House a couple of resolutions from the hospital board of the city of Winnipeg calling upon this government for a larger appropriation. At that time I believe only about $2,600 was given, and I am glad to know that the government have increased it. The hospital is carrying on a good class of work and is looking after a class of immigrants coming from the continent who would have no other protection. I would suggest that the item might be still further increased.

I would like to emphasize what my friend (Mr. Staples) has said, especially in regard to the Winnipeg hospital. It is one of the most deserving institutions in Canada. I think it is at present the largest hospital in Canada. I do not remember the proportion of foreign patients to the whole number admitted, but I believe they are in a large majority. I was through the institution a month ago and speaking to some of the head men in charge, and while they were grateful for the increased grant given them, still they felt they were not getting justice. It is a very useful institution and to-day they have not sufficient accommodation to

admit all tlie patients desiring relief. They wish to extend the hospital if they can secure the necessary aid, and I think, if the government could see its way clear to make a more liberal allowance, it would be appreciated.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I am very glaid to hear the hon. gentleman speak so highly of the hospital and of the increased grant. I was successful in getting the grant doubled last year, and I am very glad that that action is approved by gentlemen representing constituencies in the province of Manitoba. I shall be glad to use my endeavours to still further increase it, because I fully appreciate the importance of the hospital, especially located as it is at the gateway of that country, at the stopping point of all immigrants from which they diverge in all directions. It makes the claims upon the Winnipeg hospital no doubt heavier than they otherwise would be. At the same time there are claims for hospital aid all over the Northwest, which are well founded, although not as large as those of the Winnipeg hospital. While doing what we can for the Winnipeg hospital we must not do so much for it as to at all detract from the other hospitals.
What other hospitals receive grants from the Dominion government?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The following general hospitals : Moosomin, Brandon, Edmonton, Dauphin, Medicine Hat, Calgary, Battle-ford, the Holy Cross, Calgary; the Presbyterian hospital, Moosejaw; St. Paul's hospital, Saskatoon. These are aided according to the immigrant patients treated, so that of course the aid varies from year to year. I have not a statement before me, but we paid the difference between the provincial grant, whatever it may be, and one dollar a day for non-paying patients.
Did the government find it necessary to give special aid during the past winter to any settlers? For instance what has been done in different parts of Saskatchewan ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The only case occurring in Saskatchewan was at or near Lipton on the Kirkella branch. We received a letter'from the Rev. W. E. Wallace, of Stras-burg, stating that there was a somewhat unfortunate condition of affairs there. We made inquiry and by telegraph received a confirmation of that information from our sub-lands agent. We sent an officer, Mr. Wolf, from Winnipeg, to examine into the case and he reported that there was considerable necessity there. We then took measures to relieve it, much of the same nature as those mentioned in the case of Gimii and took Hens on the land.

Were special stores selected to supply these settlers, or were they allowed to buy from their own business men, so as to get the goods at the best prices?
Mr. OLIVER, I think an arrangement was made with one of the leading business men in the neighbourhood for the supply of the goods upon orders. Mr. Walker's report says that the majority, but not all of the orders, were made upon Messrs. Hasting and McLaughlin. He states that he has no personal knowledge of these gentlemen except that they appear to be reputable business men conducting a good business in the locality, and that so far as he can see their prices are not unreasonable. They were charging $2.50 and $3 a sack for flour. He says that had time and circumstances permitted the flour might have been purchased by the carload and sent from Winnipeg which would have been cheaper, but the necessities of the case required immediate relief.
Were they allowed to purchase other necessities besides flour?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I have here a list of the articles purchased by each settler. The first one purchased five sacks of flour, 50 pounds of sugar. The next purchased 14 sacks of flour, 25 pounds of pork, 14 pounds of sugar, 50 pounds of oatmeal, one pound of salt. Another one purchased 5 sacks of flour, 59 pounds of sugar, 25 pounds of beans, 25 pounds rice, &c.
If you invited competition among local storekeepers you would get more reasonable prices. Have there been complaints of excessive prices having been charged?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: No. I will send over a list of the articles and the prcies to my hon. friend.
Was any special inspection made of the settlers living northwest of Moosejaw ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I am informed we did not have any distribution east of the South Saskatchewan. That was done west of South Saskatchewan. Owing to the severity of the winter the year before last, $30,000 was voted for the relief of settlers who lived far from fuel and other facilities. This last fall fearing a repetition of the year before, we caused a pretty thorough inspection to be, made by the homestead inspectors and immigration officers, and they reported that there was no necessity for any special relief in that region. If any was given it would be given by the mounted police.
How many officers were employed in making the inspection?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Dodds, homestead inspector, Swift Current; Braun, immigration
JUN^E 5, 1908
officer, Saskatoon ; Rutfel, immigration officer, Moosejaw ; Olouston, homestead inspector, Battleford ; Roy, homestead inspector, Winnipeg, and one or two others. We tried to coyer the district as thoroughly and as quickly as possible before winter set in.
I have been informed that there are districts south of Moosejaw which are closed to all except certain classes of settlers. Is that correct?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: No instructions are given the land officers to refuse entries from any one.
Are they bound to accept the first applicant?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes. In some of the townships which have been surveyed south of Moosejaw there has been considerable delay in getting the survey plan out so that entries cannot be given, and in the meantime people have squatted there which is apt to lead to complications, although not serious.
Does the lien attach to the homestead or to the land, so that if the original homesteader left a subsequent homesteader would be subject to the lien?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The officer in the department and I do not agree as to that. He says the lien attaches to the land even though the homesteader looses the land, but my impression is that the lien is charged upon the homesteader.
Why should it not be attached to the land?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: It was the man and not the land who got the loan. If the advance were made to a private person it would attach to the land.
And why not in the case of the Crown?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Because the government is the owner of the land whether the homesteader is there or not.

The government has expended nothing on account of that homestead and it gives it as a free gift to the homesteader. In order that he may acquire a home the government makes certain advances to him which it charges as a lien against the homestead. If the homesteader is unable to pay all you have to do is to provide that the next homesteader shall take the land subject to the lien. If that is not the law it should be the law.
In my opinion it would be extremely unfair that a succeeding homesteader should be asked to pay a debt incurred by his predecessor.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I know that men who became indebted for advances many years ago were not afterwards personally re-317
lieved from liability under the lien they gave.

If you can recover it from him all right, but otherwise it should attach to the homestead. If the subsequent homesteader prefers to take that particular land with the lien on it he can do so, but otherwise he can go somewhere else, and I do not see any hardship in it. I think the government should have a lien and should enforce the lien.
Considerable advances have been made to immigrants for their maintenance after their arrival here. What progress has ibeen made in recovering those advances ?
